transcript.content: Hello, I'm Dr. Smith. It's nice to meet you. Could you tell me what brings you in to see me today?

Nice to meet you, Dr. Smith. Yeah, so... I guess I'm here because things have kind of reached a boiling point for me lately. I'm a firefighter, and you know, in that line of work, you kind of have to be ready to go from zero to sixty at the drop of a hat. You get a call, you move. But the problem with me is... well, the problem is I feel like I’m always at sixty. 

I feel like I’m just always running hot, you know? Like I have this engine inside me and I literally can’t shut the motor off. Even when we're just hanging out at the station, waiting on a call, everyone else is kicking back in the recliners or watching TV, and I just can't do it. I'm up, I'm pacing the bay, I'm reorganizing the compartments on the rig for the third time, I'm tapping my boots, I'm just constantly buzzing. 

And lately, that’s been getting me in trouble at the firehouse. My captain actually pulled me aside last shift because I'm driving everyone crazy. I just can't sit still and let things be. It's like my idle is set way too high and I don't have an off switch, and it's just... it's becoming a real issue with the guys and with my job, because I just can't ever power down.
Have you felt this way your entire life, or is this 'high-idle' state something that only started more recently?

Well, it's funny you ask that, because, I mean, I've always been a pretty active guy, you know? You don't become a firefighter if you want to sit behind a desk all day. But this specific feeling? This completely unmanageable, driving-everyone-up-the-wall kind of high-idle where I literally cannot stop moving? That is definitely more recent. 

I can actually pinpoint it pretty much exactly, to be honest with you. It’s been a real, undeniable problem for right about a year and five months now. Yeah, about seventeen months. What happened was, the department made all these changes at the station. They switched us over to these longer rotating shifts, which completely messed with whatever rhythm I had going before. You're working these weird hours, your sleep is all over the place, and just when you get used to it, the rotation flips. 

And on top of that, the brass downtown decided we needed to do way more extra documentation for every single little thing. Every call, every rig check, every time we breathe, suddenly there's a mountain of paperwork and digital logs we have to fill out. And then—and this is the real kicker—they added these new drone duties. They trained a few of us to operate the thermal drones for search and rescue and monitoring structure fires, which sounds really cool, right? But it means I'm suddenly juggling the drone maintenance, the flight logs, the regular fire gear, the paperwork, the new rotating schedule... 

And it's like my brain just kind of snapped into this permanent overdrive to try and handle it all, and now it just won't snap back. So, yeah, a year and five months of just... buzzing. Ever since they piled all that extra shift work and the documentation and the drone stuff on my plate, I just haven't been able to come back down to a normal baseline. I try to explain it to the guys, like, "Look, you gave me the drone, you gave me the logs," but it doesn't really matter to them when I'm pacing a hole in the floor at 2 AM, you know?

Beyond the friction with your colleagues at the firehouse, do you find that this constant 'buzzing' feeling is causing you significant emotional distress or interfering with other important areas of your life, like your sleep, your health, or your relationships outside of work?

Well, I mean, it's definitely bleeding into everything, but honestly, the work stuff is what's really tearing me apart right now, because... well, because it's not just the guys being annoyed with me pacing around. It's way deeper than that now. It’s actually started costing me trust at the firehouse, which, you know, in a firehouse, trust is literally everything. You have to know the guy next to you has your back and has his head in the game. 

And, see, just last week, things got so bad that I actually got pulled into a formal performance and safety meeting. The captain, the battalion chief, they all sat me down in this little sterile office, and it was brutal. Because it’s not just the buzzing—it’s that I’m so keyed up and trying to juggle the drone logs and the gear checks and all this new paperwork, and I’m just... I’m dropping the ball. I’m missing the details. Like, I’ll sign off on a rig check but forget to actually log the oxygen cylinder pressures, or I’ll misfile the drone battery maintenance report because I’m already thinking about five other things. 

And during this meeting, they basically told me that the crew feels like they can’t count on me to track the details consistently anymore. Hearing that from guys I'd walk into a burning building for... it just gutted me. I've been working so hard for the last three years to position myself for a promotion to lieutenant. I took extra classes, I did all the right things, and now... now my shot at moving into leadership feels like it’s just completely slipping through my fingers. How can they promote a guy to lead a company when his own crew doesn't trust him to fill out a safety log right? It’s just... it’s devastating. I can't sleep because I'm stressing about work, and then I go to work and I'm stressing about messing up, and my wife is always asking why I'm so on edge at home, but how do I explain that I feel like my entire career is just unravelling because I can't keep my brain in one place long enough to do my job?

Looking back at your childhood or your time in school, before you ever became a firefighter, did you ever have similar struggles with being unable to sit still, losing track of details, or feeling like your mind was constantly racing?

Yeah, actually... it's crazy you bring that up because I was just talking to my mom on the phone the other day about all this work stress, and she brought up exactly that. She basically said, "You know, you were just like this back in grade school." And... I mean, when I really sit and think about it, she's right. 

It wasn't drones and fire rigs back then, obviously, but it was the same... the same kind of chaos, I guess? Like, she reminded me how I was literally always out of my seat. The teachers would try everything—they'd put me in the back row, the front row, right next to the teacher's desk—but it didn't matter, I was just always up and wandering around the classroom or sharpening my pencil for the fifth time. And the blurting things out! Man, I would just shout the answers before the teacher even finished asking the question. It wasn't that I was trying to be a bad kid or disrespectful, it was just like... the thought hit my brain and it had to come out of my mouth immediately, zero filter, zero pause. 

And the homework... oh man, my backpack was a disaster zone. I would actually do the work, like I'd sit at the kitchen table and finish the math worksheet, and then I'd just lose it. It would get shoved into some folder and crumpled into a ball, or I'd leave it on the bus, and then my mom was constantly getting notes sent home from my teachers. It was always these little disciplinary slips or progress reports saying I was disrupting the class or missing assignments. And the most frustrating part for my parents—and for me too, honestly—was that I was bright, you know? The teachers always wrote that exact thing on the notes. They'd say, "He's bright enough to do the work, he's a smart kid, he understands the material, he just won't apply himself or sit still." 

So, yeah... I guess it's not totally a new thing. It's just that back then, the stakes were a crumpled spelling test, and now the stakes are my entire career and the safety of my crew, so it feels way, way heavier now. But that actual feeling of not being able to just stop and do things the right way? Yeah, my mom would definitely say that's been there since I was a little kid.
